item.title: Trump’s Ballroom Is Rising at Breakneck Speed: 20 Hours a Day, 7 Days a Week
item.description:
With the fate of his ballroom tied up in court, President Trump is racing against the clock.

He has enlisted a team of 250 workers to push ahead with construction 20 hours a day, seven days a week to complete as much work as quickly as possible. This week, there are plans to install one million pounds of rebar and pour 3,000 cubic yards of concrete for a project that is now two-thirds complete, the administration said in a court filing.

Now, with the matter pending before the Supreme Court, the Trump administration is making a practical appeal to the justices: The ballroom is simply too far along to be stopped now.

“His strategy clearly is to change the reality on the ground so that instead of preserving the status quo, those who rightly invoke the law against what he’s doing are put in a position of having to undo something that is already a fait accompli,” said Laurence H. Tribe, an emeritus university professor of constitutional law at Harvard.

For years, Mr. Trump has argued that the White House should have its own ballroom, saying it was a matter of prestige on the world stage. A ballroom, he said, would allow officials to hold big events for special guests without needing to erect a tent on the South Lawn.

In recent months, as preservationists and other critics have tried to halt or at least slow down the project, Mr. Trump has offered a new justification: national security. Essentially, Mr. Trump is treating the ballroom and the military bunker underneath it as one and the same.

The bunker — officially known as the Presidential Emergency Operations Center, or PEOC — was built during World War II beneath what was once the East Wing, which Mr. Trump tore down last year to make way for his ballroom.

Now, he speaks about the two projects in the same breath.

After an armed man rushed the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in April, for example, Mr. Trump said on social media that the mayhem had proved the need for “the Militarily Top Secret Ballroom currently under construction at the White House.”

Mr. Trump demolished the East Wing last October without seeking any approvals or submitting construction or demolition plans to Congress. While he did bring the project before two review panels whose leaders he had appointed, Mr. Trump has continued to change the plans from the designs they authorized.

Several federal court rulings have found that the president exceeded his authority by moving ahead without congressional approval, but the decisions have been paused pending appeals — which means the construction can go on at least until Friday, when an appeals court order to halt the aboveground construction goes into effect.

The case is also pending before the Supreme Court.

Last week, the Trump administration told the Supreme Court the president was adding flashy golden seals on the outside of the ballroom, a design element that was never submitted to the Commission of Fine Arts.

Joshua Fisher, the director of White House management and administration, told the court that a concrete-and-steel superstructure had already been built that stretches five stories deep and 70 feet high.

Mr. Fisher said 80 percent of the rebar for the project had been placed, and the concrete poured.

He said $335 million of the $400 million needed for the project had been raised from private donors. He estimated the construction was 65 percent complete.

Mr. Fisher said that the ballroom’s columns were being carved by renowned Italian artists, and that the building would be sturdy enough to withstand a nuclear blast.

“Given the current progress, the superstructure is beyond the point of return,” Mr. Fisher wrote. He added that even if the Supreme Court ordered the plans for the building altered or the building taken down, “there would be no way to do so.”

The message was clear: The ballroom cannot be undone.

But in a filing on Tuesday, the preservationists challenging the project told the justices that the administration was trying to “outrun judicial review” by suggesting that it was too late to stop the construction.

“They tell this court that because the ballroom is being built with the type of concrete used ‘in nuclear power plants,’ it will soon be ‘virtually impossible to deconstruct,’” according to the filing.

Lawyers for the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to guard America’s historic buildings, said the administration had intentionally accelerated construction “in an effort to put their illegal ballroom” beyond judicial intervention.

They have pointed to the Constitution and several federal laws that state Congress must approve such a project. One federal law says, “A building or structure shall not be erected on any reservation, park or public grounds of the federal government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”

Lower court judges have sided with the preservationists, ruling that Congress must first sign off on the expansion and renovation of the White House complex.

“Efforts to foil judicial review and arrogate Congress’s exclusive powers should not be rewarded with a stay that allows petitioners to complete a ballroom they lacked any authority to commence in the first place,” said the trust’s lawyers, led by Thaddeus A. Heuer.

In its filing on Tuesday, the trust suggested that the Supreme Court temporarily halt the aboveground work and then quickly schedule oral arguments for October or November to formally decide whether the project can proceed. If the justices do not press pause now, the trust said, the project is on track to be substantially finished this fall and it will be too late.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, has argued that the ballroom is inextricably linked to the broader national security needs of the White House complex. He said the structure is built with hardened concrete, steel and rebar; protective missile-resistant columns, roofs and beams; droneproof ceilings and roofs; and bullet-, ballistic- and blastproof glass. It includes bomb shelters, state-of-the-art hospital and medical facilities, protective partitioning between all areas of the building, top secret military structures and equipment, military-grade venting, a single integrated air conditioning and heating system, sniper nests and a drone port on top.

Mr. Sauer has also pushed back on the assertion in the unfavorable appeals court ruling that Mr. Trump is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House. “The president of the United States of America is not a tenant, but rather the sole, elected head of the executive branch,” he wrote, adding that other presidents had taken steps to renovate the White House.

The Supreme Court’s conservative majority has often been receptive to the Trump administration’s efforts to expand presidential power, but it has also ruled against some of Mr. Trump’s signature initiatives. The justices are expected to issue an order before the appeals court ruling that would halt construction takes effect on Friday.

Kimberly Wehle, a law professor at the University of Baltimore, said that Mr. Trump had been pushing to expand the powers of the presidency for years, and that attempting to construct a massive new building on White House grounds without lawmakers’ approval is his latest step.

“It’s so symbolic that he literally bulldozes the White House and says, ‘What are you going to do about it?’” she said. “They’re making this general generic argument that ‘I’m the president, so it’s national security, I can do whatever I want.’ That is a very steep, slippery slope into unlimited power in the presidency.”

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Florida Senate Candidate Angie Nixon
item.description:
State Representative Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist and union organizer, won a major upset on Tuesday in the Democratic Senate primary in Florida.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Nixon, 42, of Jacksonville, who defeated Alex Vindman, a top witness in President Trump’s first impeachment trial who vastly out-raised her. Ms. Nixon will now face Senator Ashley Moody, a Republican, in conservative-leaning Florida.

1. She is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. Ms. Nixon joined D.S.A. this year, but has downplayed her affiliation with the group, saying it is not central to her political identity. “I’m also a Democrat; I’m also a member of the Florida Public Services Union,” she said in an interview on Tuesday afternoon. The D.S.A. has notched a series of recent victories in House primaries. In the Florida primary, Ms. Nixon was also supported by some progressive House members, including Representatives Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Rashida Tlaib of Michigan and Maxwell Frost of Florida. But she was not endorsed by two of the most prominent progressives in Congress, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

2. She unseated a Democratic state lawmaker in 2020. Ms. Nixon defeated the incumbent, Kimberly Daniels, who had served two terms in the Legislature. Ms. Nixon’s campaign focused on constituent services. “I was running on being the people’s pick — the people’s champion,” she said in the interview, adding that she was heavily outspent in that race and was pregnant during the campaign. “My core campaign promise was that the constituents and Floridians would have the opportunity to reach me and talk to me.” This year, her platform calls for universal health care, higher taxes on the wealthy, abolishing for-profit prisons and raising the federal minimum wage to $25 per hour. “I believe hard-working, everyday people should really get to shape what our economies look like,” Ms. Nixon said in the interview. “Right now, Washington, D.C., is so out of touch.”

3. She was arrested while protesting a Republican redraw of her state’s House map. Ms. Nixon was a leader in Democrats’ unsuccessful efforts to stop Florida Republicans from gerrymandering the map this spring. She staged a sit-in at the office of Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, after he approved the redraw. She said she wanted to speak with the governor about the gerrymander. Instead, she was arrested. Mr. DeSantis wrote on social media that the protest was “performative nonsense.”

4. She has said her childhood was challenging. Ms. Nixon’s father, an Army veteran, was in and out of her family’s life, and her mother worked two jobs, Ms. Nixon recalled. At times, the family would stay with her grandmother. “It was stressful,” Ms. Nixon said. “It was riddled with domestic violence.” But she said her mother taught her the value of hard work.

5. She joined a rally that angered some Democrats last weekend. Ms. Nixon was one of a group of progressive candidates at a South Florida rally headlined by Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, an outspoken critic of Israel. (Ms. Nixon, like Ms. Tlaib, accuses Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza.) Some Florida Democrats objected to Ms. Tlaib’s presence, and organizers moved the event after the host venue backed out. Ms. Nixon said the event was intended to “invigorate and energize young people to get out to vote.”

item.title: Threatening Friends and Courting Enemies in Trump’s ‘Upside-Down World’
item.description:
Once again, President Trump is threatening his country’s own partners with everything from tariffs to bombs. Once again, he is fawning over a nuclear-armed tyrant deemed to be one of the biggest dangers to U.S. security. And once again, the world is left trying to make sense of a United States that has upended the world order that it established eight decades ago.

Nearly 10 years after Mr. Trump first came to the White House on the slogan of America First, his attack-thy-friends, befriend-thy-enemies approach to international relations has become the feature, not the bug, of U.S. foreign policy. Traditional alliances from Europe to Asia to the Middle East have frayed while the president courts those once seen as its adversaries.

Even so, the past few days have thrown the Trumpian worldview into stark relief. Mr. Trump declared that he would bomb Oman, a key friend in the complicated diplomacy of the Middle East, if he decides it is getting in the way of his war with Iran. He was set to impose punitive new tariffs on Canada, once considered the United States’ closest friend. And he announced that he would pull back military support from South Korea, the bulwark of the U.S. network of partners in the Asia-Pacific.

At the same time, he again began sending public mash notes to North Korea’s absolute dictator, Kim Jong-un, with whom by his own description he “fell in love” in his first term. Mr. Kim, who rules one of the most oppressive nations in the world, never did give up his nuclear weapons, as Mr. Trump once declared he would. Instead, Mr. Kim has vastly expanded his nuclear arsenal in defiance of Mr. Trump, who nonetheless remains a suitor, no matter how unrequited.

“He dumps on our friends and cozies up to our enemies,” said James J. Blanchard, a former ambassador to Canada and Democratic governor of Michigan. “If someone once told me that Russia is our friend and Canada is our enemy, I’d have told you we’re in an upside-down world.”

Richard Fontaine, the chief executive of the Center for a New American Security and a former adviser to Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona, said that none of the bombastic threats were new. But he pointed out that Mr. Trump had not always followed through on them. The United States, he noted, had not pulled out of NATO, abandoned South Korea, bombed Oman or seized Canada and Greenland.

“Increasingly, the bullying rhetoric is being priced in by countries around the world,” Mr. Fontaine said. “They don’t dismiss it, but they don’t take the threats literally either. As more and more unfulfilled threats are issued, people listen less. It undermines the president’s credibility.”

Mr. Trump has long argued that his approach to other countries, however unorthodox, makes sense for the United States. Under previous presidents, allies took advantage of America’s security presence and trade rules without reciprocating, Mr. Trump maintains. He sees relatively high trade deficits and relatively low NATO military spending as proof that so-called friends are exploiting the United States.

As for sweet talking North Korea, China, Russia and other longtime adversaries, Mr. Trump contends that the confrontational policies of the past failed to achieve what they set out to, so better to try more diplomacy. He still hopes to reach a nuclear accord with North Korea, seal a comprehensive trade deal with China and reestablish full ties with Russia by brokering an end to Moscow’s war in Ukraine. He has pushed aides for a meeting this fall with Mr. Kim, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The war with Iran has provided a new scorecard for the allies that deserve support and those that do not. Countries that have declined to facilitate military operations against Tehran or use force to help guarantee passage through the Strait of Hormuz have in his view betrayed the United States, even though he never asked for their opinions before starting the war. After targeting Britain, France, Spain, Italy and others for not doing more to help him against Iran, Mr. Trump has now focused his ire on South Korea.

“We have 39,000 soldiers over there guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbor, and you’re not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran?” he said this week after announcing that he would scale back joint exercises with South Korea.

By contrast, he went on, “Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect, and we’ve met on numerous occasions, actually, two primary occasions — spoken and spent time. I understand him. He understands me.”

If so, that distinguishes Mr. Kim from European and Asian allies who still do not understand Mr. Trump, even if they have come to expect his volatile outbursts. Until now, presidents of both parties have valued their relationships with overseas friends. And while there have been plenty of moments of tension over the years, they have worked to keep them from escalating too far.

Now the allies are the ones trying to avoid exacerbating the situation. “They grit their teeth and bear it because in the end they do not want to see irreparable damage done to the alliance over the next two years,” said Victor D. Cha, the president of the Geopolitics and Foreign Policy Department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “In short, allies may like and trust the U.S. less today, but they still need the U.S.”

Mr. Cha, who was an Asia adviser to President George W. Bush, said that President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea actually has a good relationship with Mr. Trump and does not want to harm that. “Lee is also as transactional as Trump, so if Trump’s outreach to Kim Jong-un works, that is very much in South Korea’s interests,” Mr. Cha said.

The presence of U.S. forces in South Korea since the 1950s war has long irritated Mr. Trump, who sees it in zero-sum terms. In his first term, he sought to pull troops out and cancel military exercises, judging them wasteful and unnecessarily provocative toward his friend in North Korea. He sought to charge South Korea billions of dollars for U.S. protection, and linked security issues to his complaints about Seoul’s trade policies.

Mr. Trump is not the first president interested in bringing troops home from South Korea so long after the war. President Jimmy Carter promised to scale down U.S. forces there, but gave up amid resistance from Congress and his own administration. Donald H. Rumsfeld, who was Mr. Bush’s defense secretary, surprised the South Koreans by redeploying a brigade to Iraq, and never returned it. Today, about 28,500 U.S. troops are stationed in South Korea, according to the Congressional Research Service.

“There could be a strategic case for restructuring the U.S. military presence on the peninsula,” said Michael J. Green, the chief executive of the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney in Australia, “but none for making them a pawn in a flirtation with the world’s cruelest dictator — particularly at a time when North Koreans are coming back from the Ukraine war battle hardened and backed by a larger missile inventory than they had in 2018.”

Oman, for its part, has for years been an important interlocutor between the United States and Iran, helping to facilitate negotiations when the two sides were open to talks. But Mr. Trump has grown increasingly aggravated that Oman has sought to broker a deal with Iran to control the Strait of Hormuz.

He first threatened to mount an unprovoked war on the sultanate in May, saying that “Oman will behave just like everybody else or we’ll have to blow them up.” On Monday, he lashed out again, declaring that if Oman “gets in the way” of his efforts to reach an agreement with Iran, “we’ll bomb the shit out of them.”

Canada faces a different form of hostility from Mr. Trump, who vowed to slap new tariffs of 50 percent on more than 500 Canadian goods, including hockey sticks and cheese, Tuesday at midnight. Just 90 minutes before his self-imposed deadline, Mr. Trump, as he often has done, pulled back from the brink and suspended the tariffs for three days to give more time for talks.

But even if the two sides eventually reach an accord, there remain many points of friction between the neighbors, exacerbated by Mr. Trump’s oft-expressed ambition to take over Canada and make it “the 51st state.” Just last month, the opening of the new Gordie Howe International Bridge linking Detroit with Windsor, Ontario, was delayed for weeks over various grievances Mr. Trump has with Canada.

Mr. Blanchard said he suspected that the latest eruptions against Canada and other U.S. allies stemmed from Mr. Trump’s inability to bring the Iran war to a close. Neither bombing nor negotiations have forced Iran to surrender control of the Strait of Hormuz or to make verifiable commitments to abandon its nuclear program. The president appears stuck in a geopolitical trap without a clear path forward.

Mr. Fontaine said that Mr. Trump’s approach to allies and adversaries undermined U.S. interests. “There should be benefits to being a friend of America, and costs for being an enemy,” he said, “not the other way around.”

item.title: Haitians in Springfield Hunker Down as ICE Begins Detentions
item.description:
Federal agents have been detaining small numbers of Haitians over the last week in Springfield, Ohio, according to community leaders and advocates, fueling widespread fear among the immigrants that is prompting many to stay home.

At least 15 Haitians have been detained by federal agents, who have been in the city almost every day since early last week, the local leaders said. More than 100 others have been summoned in recent weeks to Immigration and Customs Enforcement offices miles away, where they have been fitted with electronic ankle monitors that track their movements.

Springfield has been on edge since the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to terminate Temporary Protected Status, a program that shielded 330,000 Haitians nationwide from deportation and granted them legal work authorization.

“People in our community are terrified,” said Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Springfield Haitian Support Center, the local organization that supports Haitians.

“It’s extremely chaotic,” he said. “We have people isolating themselves, refusing to eat.”

The Department of Homeland Security declined to answer questions about enforcement operations in Springfield.

“Every day, D.H.S. is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe,” the department said in a statement. “D.H.S. does not discuss ongoing or future operations.”

ICE has indicated internally that it would push to quickly deport people who recently lost T.P.S., including those from Haiti, Syria, Yemen and South Sudan.

In guidance sent to ICE officers last week and reviewed by The New York Times, the agency said former T.P.S. holders should “first be considered for expedited removal,” a process that allows the government to deport certain immigrants without court proceedings.

The D.H.S. did not respond to a request for comment on the guidance.

In June, a federal appeals court allowed the Trump administration to resume using the fast-track deportation process nationwide. Under previous administrations, expedited removal was used narrowly for undocumented migrants detained near the southern border. But the Trump administration has pushed to expand federal use of this authority.

In Springfield, the support center’s usually crowded waiting room was deserted on Tuesday as word spread that roving unmarked SUVs and a van in a parking lot had been identified as ICE vehicles by volunteers patrolling the streets.

Even as they hunker down, Haitians have been calling the center nonstop seeking answers, said Mr. Dorsainvil. Is it too risky to go to work? How can I get to Canada? What will become of my children if I am arrested?

One of the few people there on Tuesday was Marie, 63, who had an ankle monitor clamped around her leg. A Springfield resident for more than five years, she lost her right to work when T.P.S. ended. She had come to check if it was too late to apply for asylum. (Petitions normally must be filed within one year of entering the country.)

“I am petrified of being deported to Haiti,” she said. “I talked to my family there just yesterday, and they told me they hear gunshots day and night.”

Another visitor, Lucson, 35, supports a wife and two young daughters in Haiti by working at a local auto-parts manufacturer under a work permit tied to his pending asylum application. But he sees the toll around him: Roughly 20 Haitian co-workers were let go when T.P.S. ended, and others have stayed away from work entirely as ICE activity ramped up.

Both immigrants asked to be identified solely by their first names out of fear of retribution from U.S. authorities.

Inside St. Vincent de Paul, a Catholic charity, American volunteers packed food boxes for delivery to Haitian families, many of whom had never needed aid before, said Casey Rollins, the executive director.

“We are taking care of people forced out of their jobs,” said Ms. Rollins, her eye welling with tears.

Haitian residents also require assistance with utilities and rent payments, she said.

Only two families were at the charity, where parents have also been receiving help filling out passport applications for their American-born children and granting power of attorney to trusted friends who could take custody of their children if they are detained.

Springfield, a struggling industrial town for decades, was revitalized by thousands of Haitians who began settling here in recent years after hearing that jobs were plentiful and the cost of living affordable.

The city, home to 10,000 to 15,000 Haitians, was thrust into the contentious immigration debate after President Trump said from the debate stage in September 2024 that the newcomers to the city were eating their neighbors’ pets.

Once in office, his administration moved to strip Temporary Protected Status from Haitians and others. The protection is offered to foreigners already in the United States when conditions are considered too dangerous for safe return to their home countries.

Lower courts ruled that the Trump administration had been motivated by racial animus and had failed to conduct the required assessment of conditions on the ground in Haiti, which has been struggling with political instability, gang violence and food insecurity. But the Supreme Court decided in late June that the administration had the authority to end the program.

Since then, the Trump administration has been under pressure to start rounding up Haitians.

The arrests in Springfield have drawn less attention nationally than the operations in cities like Minneapolis, Chicago and Los Angeles, where federal agents descended in large numbers.

“ICE hasn’t been here on a large scale but their daily raids are scaring people and disrupting the peace of the city,” said Carl Ruby, the pastor of Central Christian Church, founder of a coalition of churches that has organized to protect Haitians.

And the arrests have been random, rather than targeted, he and others said.

Small groups of agents have been detaining immigrants in Springfield as they leave their homes or commute to or from work.

“If they focused on the worst of the worst as they claim, we could support that,” said Mr. Ruby. “Their real goal is to incite fear, hoping that people will go back to Haiti.”

Vulder Marco Dorsainvil, 30, who is a permanent legal resident and Mr. Dorsainvil’s brother, said agents followed him from his apartment complex to a Kroger parking lot, where they boxed in his car between three unmarked vehicles. They released him after he produced a green card.

“They were looking for anybody to take,” he said. “They didn’t know my name.”

Mr. Ruby said that as he watched ICE agents arrest two people on Monday, one of the agents tried to hand him a small figure of Jesus.

“Jesus didn’t want people to hand out meaningless tokens,” Mr. Ruby said. “He wants us to welcome and care for the vulnerable.”

Hamed Aleaziz and Madeleine Ngo contributed reporting.

item.title: Democratic State Representative Scores Upset Win in Florida Senate Primary
item.description:
State Representative Angie Nixon of Jacksonville, a progressive firebrand who ran an underdog campaign, won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Florida, according to The Associated Press, the latest left-wing victory against establishment Democrats.

In a huge upset, Ms. Nixon, 42, defeated Alex Vindman, a former national security official who was a top witness in President Trump’s first impeachment trial. His entry was largely welcomed by Democratic Party leaders hoping to make Florida, which leans right, at least competitive this fall. Mr. Vindman far out-raised Ms. Nixon and was the clear front-runner in the race.

But there was no public polling ahead of the primary. Pollsters most likely saw little upside to spending money in a state that President Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024.

Ms. Nixon, a union organizer, ran a grass-roots campaign, often driving herself to events across the state — clad in her signature hot pink outfits — and relying on volunteers and union members for field organizing. In a low-turnout primary, they bet that reaching enough Democratic voters directly, and talking to them about issues such as unaffordable health care and child care, would drive them to the polls to support Ms. Nixon.

The strategy succeeded: Ms. Nixon defeated Mr. Vindman across Florida’s urban counties, including Miami-Dade and Broward, where Mr. Vindman has lived since he moved to the state in 2023.

“We came up short, but we have Angie Nixon,” Mr. Vindman told supporters inside an American Legion hall near Fort Lauderdale in his concession speech on Tuesday night. “Rep. Nixon ran a strong campaign. She challenged the status quo. She put in the hard work, and tonight, she earned the nomination.”

Ms. Nixon rolled to victory despite an enormous fund-raising disparity. She raised about $975,000 during the campaign, while Mr. Vindman, powered by a national donor network, raised $16.3 million. Mr. Vindman was so confident in winning Tuesday that he had a fund-raiser scheduled for Sunday in Nantucket, Mass., as he prepared for a costly general election.

That general election will now happen without him.

Ms. Nixon acknowledged the spending gap in her victory speech at her watch party in Jacksonville. “We have proved that everyday people are more powerful than corporations and billionaires,” she said, after being introduced by her mother.

“We were outspent 16 to 1, and we won,” she added. “This win was for the little guys and girls.”

Ms. Nixon, who joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June, will now test whether a progressive can win over moderate Democrats, as well as independents and crossover Republicans, in an increasingly red state.

She will challenge Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, in November.

In Jacksonville, where Ms. Nixon held her watch party, a big crowd jumped as they watched the results on television. “This is what democracy looks like,” they chanted.

“She’s for the people,” said Kaydene Williams, who attended the party. “She makes herself available to the people.”

Although Ms. Moody is the sitting senator, Democrats see her as potentially vulnerable in a tough midterm year for Republicans. She has held the position only since last year, having been appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, after Marco Rubio left the post to become secretary of state. She remains little known among Florida voters, polls show, even after winning two terms as the state’s attorney general.

But Republicans have clear structural advantages in Florida elections, including more robust fund-raising and field organization. And Democrats have tended to bet on moderates to unseat Republican incumbents.

Ms. Nixon, who is the clear underdog to Ms. Moody in the Florida Senate race, said in a brief interview with The New York Times on Tuesday night that she would defy expectations in November the same way she had won the Democratic primary: “By going out and having conversations with people.”

“They are going to lie and call me all kinds of names,” she added. “If I want to profess to be the next U.S. senator, I have to meet people where they are and talk to them.”

Susan Cooper Eastman contributed reporting from Jacksonville, Fla.

item.title: David Jolly Wins Democratic Nomination for Florida Governor
item.description:
Former Representative David Jolly, a Republican turned Democrat and a strong critic of President Trump, won the Democratic nomination for Florida governor on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.

Mr. Jolly, 53, will be the underdog in the general-election race to replace Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican who has solidified the state as a conservative stronghold.

Mr. Jolly defeated the second-placed finisher, Dayna Marie Foster, a liberal former teacher from Fort Lauderdale who was endorsed by Florida’s Democratic Progressive Caucus. Placing third was State Representative Dotie Joseph of North Miami, who entered the race late to give Democrats a more progressive choice. An earlier contender, Mayor Jerry Demings of Orange County, home to Orlando, dropped out of the race before the qualifying deadline, citing a cancer diagnosis.

Mr. Jolly, a lawyer, served as a Republican congressman from 2014 to 2017. He left the Republican Party in 2018 and has been a frequent political commentator on cable news. He held no party affiliation until registering as a Democrat last year.

Although Florida was a hotly contested political battleground for years, registered Republicans in the state now handily outnumber Democrats. The party has not won a governor’s race since 1994, although Democrats came close eight years ago when Andrew Gillum, a Democrat, narrowly lost to Mr. DeSantis.

In an expensive state with multiple media markets, Representative Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate for governor endorsed by Mr. Trump, has raised more than $100 million, far surpassing Mr. Jolly’s $10 million.

Still, Mr. Jolly has sought to tie Republicans to the broader voter discontent with Mr. Trump that helped Democrats win two special elections in Florida this year. Mr. Jolly has positioned himself as a moderate who will attack the state’s affordability crisis. And he is betting on voters to be fatigued by the culture battles waged by Mr. DeSantisAt a rally on Tuesday in Miami Lakes, Fla., Mr. Jolly urged voters in November to reject divisive rhetoric in favor of a government that is both lean and compassionate. “We are celebrating the return of a resiliency, the renewal of a hope, the belief in each other once again,” Mr. Jolly said.

He also cast Mr. Donalds as beholden to big-money corporate interests. “Everybody in this state can pull up a chair to the table. But money doesn’t buy access,” Mr. Jolly said.

David C. Adams contributed reporting from Miami Lakes, Fla.

item.title: ‘With All My Heart, Natalie.’ Trump’s Most Devoted Aide Emerges.
item.description:
She never takes a day off, not even on Sunday. She works out of the Oval Office and she’s got a regular seat on Marine One. She texts with world leaders on the president’s behalf. She stays up late with him drafting social media posts.

She rarely speaks on camera and yet she is never not there, ever-present with a wide smile and her eyes fixed on the president.

She is Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old West Wing aide who is the utmost gatekeeper to President Trump, a one-woman conduit of information operating entirely outside the usual chain of command. The public’s interest in Ms. Harp exploded after she was revealed last week to be one of the lucky few who joined the president inside an airplane catering container to be whisked out of Turkey under threat of attack by Iran.

This week she became the subject of a political attack line delivered by Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator from Georgia, who said of the president: “He doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.”

The senator’s singling out of Ms. Harp triggered a particularly ferocious response from many corners of Trump world. White House aides, lawmakers on Capitol Hill, conservative influencers and at least one cabinet member took to the ramparts on X to defend Ms. Harp’s honor. There were accusations of sexism from the right and cries of snowflakery from the left. Mr. Trump deflected when a reporter from CNN asked him about Mr. Ossoff’s comments. But a social media account run by the administration then attacked the reporter in unusually personal terms, invoking her children.

The furor intensified the spotlight on this seldom-heard-from and sylphlike woman who has long fascinated and frustrated people around the president. This article is based on interviews with a half-dozen people with knowledge of her role. Ms. Harp did not respond to a request for comment.

The unique power Mr. Trump affords her says much about how he functions as president.

As long as Ms. Harp is around, he enjoys an unvetted flow of information, some of it poisonous and counterproductive, at least as far as a number of his other advisers are concerned. She supplies him with content she fishes out of the social media gutter (like the video he posted depicting the Obamas as apes) and provides him with a view from the world outside official Washington, of which he has always been mistrustful. Her moniker is “the human printer,” because she tails the president with a portable printer so she can hand him information in hard copy.

She is a platinum blonde geyser of positivity, there to buck him up when the going gets rough. She believes, or at least vehemently claims to believe, that he totally won the 2020 election. In the book “Regime Change,” by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, Mr. Trump is described as explaining to people that Ms. Harp is the only one who loves him as much as his wife and children. All his other staff will go off and make money, Mr. Trump would say, but Ms. Harp will never leave him.

“Natalie Harp is one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on President Trump’s team,” Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary who will soon be leaving her post, said in response to questions from The Times about the nature of Ms. Harp’s position and why she was chosen to join the president on the secret food-delivery-truck rescue gambit.

In some ways, Ms. Harp is filling a role that Mr. Trump has always required, going back to his days as a real estate developer in Manhattan. Back then, there were always secretaries sitting outside his office on the 26th floor of Trump Tower, ready at a moment’s notice to hop to it. He referred to these women as “the girls.”

Ms. Harp collects a taxpayer-funded salary of $150,000. Her double-barreled title is special assistant to the president and executive assistant to the president. At work she can be a bit of a loner. Even in this West Wing, in which loyalty to the president seems to know no bounds, Ms. Harp’s displays of devotion have unnerved some of her colleagues.

Several videos shared with The Times show Ms. Harp sprinting across great distances to keep up with Mr. Trump’s golf cart as it putters across his course in Scotland. “I also am sorry if I was an embarrassment walking the course in Scotland,” she wrote in a letter to the president that was viewed by The Times.

The letter goes on to say: “I want things to always be right between us. I also know I’ve been distracted all week (forgetting to eat throughout the days, and even forgetting to sleep, and only catching a couple hours at a time).”

The letter concludes: “With all my heart, Natalie.”

She grew up in California. On Wednesday, her brother, with whom she is apparently estranged, gave an interview to CNN. He said this about his sister: “I’d say since she was, like, 16, she’s had an obsession with, um, gosh, how do I explain this? Um, she’s written letters to other presidents, let me put it that way.” (He said he was referring to George W. Bush.)

Ms. Harp’s connection to this president runs deep. She credits him with saving her life.

She has said that she suffered from bone cancer and that it was legislation Mr. Trump signed in 2018 that provided her access to experimental treatments. (She has not publicly detailed which treatments.)

She was recounting that experience on Fox News in 2019 when she caught the president’s eye. He invited her to speak at the Republican National Convention in 2020. She spent the next two years repeating his election lies as an anchor on the far-right One America News Network. In 2022, she finally joined his team.

A “War Room”-style documentary filmed during Mr. Trump’s 2024 campaign, called “Art of the Surge,” provides glimpses of Ms. Harp hard at work.

“Politics was never something I liked,” she explains in one scene that was filmed at Mar-a-Lago. “But when I was sick, I started watching the Republican debates. He was my first exposure to politics, and I loved it. Like, this guy, he gets it.”

The film cuts to Mr. Trump introducing Ms. Harp in 2019 at something called the Faith & Freedom Coalition’s “Road to Majority” conference.

“They were preparing her for death,” he says. “Her name is Natalie Harp, and because of ‘right to try,’ she’s now living, and I think doing phenomenally well. And somebody said she’s here. Are you here, Natalie? Where’s Natalie? Will you come up here, please?”

The woman who walks across the stage to hug him is not yet the full-fledged Trump aide she would soon become.

“I had cancer and he saved my life, signed that bill,” she says in the film, “and ever since he found out, he stayed in touch with me. Made sure I was OK.”

item.title: Harriet Hageman, Backed by Trump, Wins G.O.P. Senate Primary in Wyoming
item.description:
Representative Harriet Hageman, a close ally of President Trump’s, won the Republican primary race for Senate in Wyoming on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.

Ms. Hageman, who rose to prominence four years ago by defeating Representative Liz Cheney, will be an overwhelming general-election favorite in Wyoming, one of the most conservative states.

Ms. Hageman, 63, is running to replace Senator Cynthia Lummis, a retiring Republican. Ms. Lummis endorsed Ms. Hageman in January, describing her as a “real workhorse” and a strong champion for Mr. Trump’s agenda.

Ms. Hageman, a daughter of a state lawmaker, is campaigning on a pledge to fight what she casts as federal government overreach into water rights and private property rights in Wyoming. She was also endorsed by the Wyoming Republican Party and by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the nation’s largest business lobbying group.

Mr. Trump endorsed her by late December, immediately establishing her as an all but prohibitive favorite in Wyoming. He carried the state by 46 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, his largest margin of victory in any state.

In 2021, Mr. Trump supercharged the House candidacy of Ms. Hageman, a Cheyenne trial lawyer who had only a small political following before Mr. Trump backed her bid to unseat Ms. Cheney, one of his fiercest Republican critics.

Before her House run, Ms. Hageman had served as a Republican National Committee official, and also lost in a 2018 run for the Wyoming governorship. She once was an ally of Ms. Cheney’s and a critic of a Mr. Trump’s, even referring to him in 2016 as “racist and xenophobic,” but by 2020 had transformed into a fervent supporter.

After Mr. Trump lost the 2020 presidential election, she amplified his false claims that the election had been rigged. She has called him the “greatest president” of her lifetime.

With Mr. Trump’s support, she thundered past Ms. Cheney in 2022, winning by more than 37 points. Ms. Cheney — whose father, Dick Cheney, was President George W. Bush’s powerful vice president — had become one of Mr. Trump’s top targets for retribution after she helped lead the House panel investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.

Ms. Hageman said Wyoming was “fed up with the Jan. 6 commission” and “fed up with Liz Cheney.”

Although Ms. Hageman’s primary race for Senate this year was not competitive, Mr. Trump continued to issue statements of support for her into the final month of the race, in which she faced a group of long-shot challengers.

“Harriet has ALWAYS delivered for Wyoming,” he wrote on social media in early August, “and will continue to do so in the United States Senate.”

item.title: Rancher Beats Trump-Backed Candidate in Primary for Governor of Wyoming
item.description:
Eric Barlow, a rancher and state senator in Wyoming, won the Republican primary for governor on Tuesday, The Associated Press said, beating a candidate endorsed by President Trump in one of the country’s most staunchly Republican states.

Mr. Barlow’s victory means he is all but certain to become the next governor of Wyoming, where Republicans hold every statewide office, and voters gave Mr. Trump his largest margin of victory in the 2024 presidential election.

This year, legislative races in Wyoming have turned into a contest between the right and far right as ultraconservative candidates pushed to take control of the State Senate, where more moderate Republicans have held sway. Mr. Barlow ran a campaign that focused on problem solving and lowering the temperature of Wyoming’s internecine Republican brawls, in contrast to his Trump-endorsed rival, Megan Degenfelder, who promised to stock state agencies with “bulldogs.” He also defeated Brent Bien, a far-right conservative and retired Marine Corps colonel who won the endorsement of the Wyoming Republican Party.

Mr. Barlow’s victory suggested that Wyoming’s heavily Republican electorate preferred a lower-key leader similar to the incumbent governor, Mark Gordon, rather than a bomb-throwing conservative or culture warrior. Mr. Gordon, a mainstream Republican, is leaving office after two terms.

His win also showed the limits of Mr. Trump’s power to tilt a Republican primary in a sparsely populated rural state where many voters make up their minds by chatting with candidates at barbecues, county fairs and rodeos.

Ms. Degenfelder, Wyoming’s state superintendent of public instruction, touted the president’s support, her battles “against the radicals’ agenda” and her advocacy of the state’s ban on transgender athletes in girls’ sports.

Mr. Barlow is widely expected to win in November against the Democratic nominee, Ken Casner, a Vietnam veteran who runs a retail shop and cafe.

Mr. Barlow, often sporting a white cowboy hat, ran as a “fourth-generation ranch kid” who served in the Marines before rising through the ranks of Wyoming politics, where he spent two years as speaker of the State House.

Mr. Barlow emphasized his support for public lands — an issue that unites conservative hunters and liberal environmentalists in the American West — and vowed to change the tone of Wyoming’s increasingly bitter politics.

In one memorable video critical of the negative mailers swamping voters, Mr. Barlow — who is also a veterinarian — pulled on a long plastic glove, reached into a mailbox and retrieved a pile of yak dung.

Mr. Barlow and Ms. Degenfelder promised a continuation of the Republican policies that have dominated Wyoming for years. Both oppose abortion, and they vowed to support the mining and energy industries that drive much of the state’s economy while also shoring up its struggling rural health care systems.

item.title: Pentagon Scales Back Major Training Exercises With South Korea
item.description:
The Pentagon said late on Tuesday that it was ending a major training exercise with South Korea one week earlier than scheduled, on Aug. 21, and scaling back many remaining live-fire training drills to computer simulations or canceling them altogether.

The moves came after President Trump on Sunday ordered the Defense Department to reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, a longtime U.S. ally and a linchpin of America’s national security strategy in the Asia-Pacific region.

Mr. Trump’s order was aimed at rekindling talks with Kim Jong-un of North Korea at a time when efforts to resolve the Iran war have hit an impasse, as well as punishing the South Koreans for declining to join in the conflict against Iran, a position that deeply angered Mr. Trump.

In a statement released on Tuesday night, the Pentagon said it was sharply curtailing the 11-day training exercise in South Korea, called Ulchi Freedom Shield, “while continuing training that enhances tactical capability.”

“These adjustments preserve essential readiness and training objectives,” the statement continued. “There will be no degradation to U.S. training objectives.”

Even before the Pentagon’s announcement, Mr. Trump’s order had heightened fears among Asian allies over what the United States is now willing to do to deter China in its territorial ambitions, given the enormous distraction and resource drain of the Iran war. The United States is running low on crucial weapons and has been moving military resources from Asia to the Middle East.

Current and former U.S. military commanders have said that abruptly scaling back the duration of the exercise and converting many of its live-fire components to computer simulations would not only stoke those fears but also erode American military readiness on the highly militarized Korean Peninsula.

In Seoul on Wednesday, ⁠South Korea’s foreign minister, Cho Hyun, said at a parliamentary ⁠hearing that neither his country nor the United States had been given advance warning about Mr. Trump’s order on Sunday to scale back joint military drills.“Neither our government nor U.S. officials had any prior knowledge of what President Trump revealed,” Mr. Cho said. “We received no advance notice.”

The exercises are held most summers with South Korea’s armed forces and with other U.S. allies in the Asia-Pacific region. They focus on how the allied militaries can counter a wide range of security threats, including drones and cyberattacks, while also strengthening combined defenses. They are designed to help U.S. allies defend against threats from North Korea.

Col. Ryan Donald, director of public affairs for the Combined Forces Command, United Nations Command and U.S. Forces Korea, said in a news conference with the South Korean on Aug. 10 that the exercises reflected the changing character of war, including the growing use of unmanned systems, electronic warfare and cyberoperations.

In the convoluted social media post, Mr. Trump complained on Sunday that Seoul did not “join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” In the same post, he said that North Korea under Mr. Kim had been “unthreatening and respectful” while he has been president.The U.S. and South Korean militaries have held joint exercises for more than 70 years, since 1955, after the 1953 armistice that ended the Korean War.

item.title: Unusual Spending Raises Prospect of Election Meddling in Alaska
item.description:
In Alaska’s primary on Tuesday, not all ads may be as they seem. Don’t assume that all of the commercials boosting Republican candidates are backed by the G.O.P. or that spots promoting Democrats are backed by Democratic money.

That’s because the ascendant trend of election meddling — in which partisans try to shape the outcome by boosting a fringe candidate, or one seen as less formidable, from the other party in hopes of elevating a likely loser into the general election — appears to have gone into overdrive in the 49th state. And Alaska’s unique primary, in which the top four candidates advance to the general election, has added another dimension to the ad wars.

About $800,000 has been spent in the last few weeks by the super PAC Fair Deal Alaska to not only attack the leading Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, but also boost two lesser-known hopefuls, the Green Party candidate Richard Grayson (who lives in Arizona) and Carol Hafner, another Democrat who could pull votes away from Ms. Peltola. That could benefit the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan Sullivan. Fair Deal Alaska formed just late last month, meaning its donors have not yet been disclosed.

Not to be outdone, another $2.2 million has come from a super PAC called Right for Alaska to oppose Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and also boost long-shot candidates, Alaskan Party member Earl Southworth and Republican Jerry Heikes, both of whom could pull votes from Mr. Sullivan.

And then over the final two weeks, another $300,000 has been spent by the American Democracy Project, a third super PAC, to support David Leslie, a Democrat.

The groups did not respond to requests for comment.

Some of the hangers-on have voiced surprise in media interviews that there are apparently well-funded super PACs spending on their behalf.

Alaska’s newish primary system, in which the top four candidates advance from Tuesday’s primary into the general election, makes the state especially ripe for subterfuge. Aside from the surge in super PAC spending, there have been accusations that one candidate — a different Dan Sullivan — is a plant meant to siphon support from the incumbent.

Alaska also uses ranked-choice voting in the general election as part of its new system.

In a close race, as the matchup between Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan (the sitting senator) is expected to be, the partisan leanings of which candidates take the other two general spots could shape whether Republicans or Democrats control the seat — and perhaps the U.S. Senate itself.

item.title: ‘I’m Not That Informed on National Security,’ Graham Says in South Carolina Debate
item.description:
At the only debate in a runoff election that will most likely determine the next senator from South Carolina, Senator Darline Graham stumbled over a question about the importance of Taiwan to U.S. interests, saying she was “not that informed on national security.”

The awkward moment, which prompted boos from the audience, underscored her biggest vulnerability in the race to succeed her brother, the late Lindsey Graham. Ms. Graham has the full support of President Trump, but she lacks the experience of her opponent, Representative Ralph Norman, who easily explained why Taiwan is an economic ally for the United States and worth protecting against China.

On Tuesday night from an opera house in Newberry, S.C., the candidates offered voters a stark contrast in their leadership styles. Aside from the foreign-policy stumble, Ms. Graham appeared poised and portrayed herself as a loyal ally to Mr. Trump. Mr. Norman, the vice chairman of the Freedom Caucus and five-term congressman, flexed his ultraconservative record to argue that he would defend the interests of South Carolinians, even if it meant breaking with the president.

Here are five takeaways from the debate. Early voting starts on Wednesday, ahead of the special Republican primary election on Aug. 25.

It was in response to a question about whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are of national-security interest to the United States that Ms. Graham drew a blank.

“I’m just going to be honest here,” she said. “I’m not that informed on national security.”

Gasps and boos could be heard in the audience. Mr. Graham, among the Senate’s most hawkish defenders of U.S. national security, had dedicated his Senate career to foreign policy issues.

Ms. Graham offered that she supported the military and then leaned on her oft-repeated argument for voters who doubted her qualifications to serve in the Senate: Her status as a political outsider is an asset.

“I’m not a polished politician up here,” she said.

Ms. Graham has sought to differentiate herself from her brother by saying she is more focused on domestic issues that directly affect people like her.

One of her strongest moments came when she recounted living off Social Security benefits after her parents died during her childhood. She also animated the room during her closing statement, when she hit Mr. Norman — who ran for governor earlier this year — for not knowing whether he wanted to be in South Carolina or Washington.

Mr. Norman, who endorsed Nikki Haley in her 2024 presidential bid against Mr. Trump, appears to have little to lose when it comes to his relationship with the president.

Mr. Trump not only has endorsed Ms. Graham, but also has been working steadily to rally support around her in the sprint to the runoff next Tuesday. He will appear with her at a rally on Friday in Myrtle Beach.

On Tuesday night, Mr. Norman said he generally supported Mr. Trump’s goals in the war, but he also thought the president owed Americans an explanation for why it was ongoing.

“He’s going to have to tell the American people what it’s going to take if the Straits of Hormuz are still dominated by a country that’s supposed to be decimated,” he said.

For most of the debate, Ms. Graham was consistently on the attack.

She knocked him for voting to raise state gas taxes while he served in the state legislature and criticized him for accepting federal bailout funds during the coronavirus pandemic, even as he voted against stimulus checks for millions of Americans.

Mr. Norman defended his record, but he seemed intent, at least at the start, to avoid engaging with her jabs. He grew more aggressive as the debate came to a close. In one moment that energized the crowd, he criticized Ms. Graham for her affiliation with a PAC funded largely by a Democratic donor.

Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, the government’s top Covid adviser during the pandemic, should “be in an orange jumpsuit,” Mr. Norman said. Illegal immigrants should be “immediately deported,” Ms. Graham said. Both agreed that the Senate should pass a voting restriction bill that Mr. Trump had demanded for months.

Still, they differed on some issues.

On health care, Mr. Norman touted a free-market solution that would allow consumers to purchase insurance plans across state lines, while Ms. Graham discussed the importance of increasing funding for rural hospitals. Both took a hard line on immigration policy — an opportunity for Ms. Graham to distinguish herself from her brother’s more moderate stance.

Just about every time Ms. Graham tried to contest his record, Mr. Norman offered this one-line retort:

“It’s silly season, folks.”

He deployed the line repeatedly to avoid sparring with his opponent, presenting himself as more experienced, while perhaps also avoiding the optics of attacking the grieving sister of a longtime fixture of South Carolina politics.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Alaska Senate Candidate Mary Peltola
item.description:
Mary Peltola, an Alaska Native and moderate former congresswoman running on a platform she describes as “fish, family and freedom,” is the leading Democrat in Alaska’s nonpartisan primary election on Tuesday.

The top four finishers regardless of party will advance to the general election in November. To have a shot at taking back control of the Senate, Democrats almost certainly will need Ms. Peltola to beat Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Peltola.

Ms. Peltola’s father, Ward Sattler, a teacher and bush pilot, moved to Alaska from Nebraska. Her mother, LizAnn Piicigaq Williams, was a member of the Yup’ik group of Indigenous peoples of western Alaska. Ms. Peltola grew up along the Kuskokwim River near the Bering Sea, fishing for salmon, picking berries and eating seal and moose meat. In 1995, she won the Miss National Congress of American Indians pageant, a competition in which she wore a squirrel skin parka and a wolf hair headdress.

Ms. Peltola, 52, grew up going to events for Don Young, the longtime Republican congressman, because her father was friends with him. After attending four different colleges — she never graduated — she ran for the State House in 1996 and lost. She ran again in 1998 and won. Representing Bethel, 400 miles from Anchorage and nearly 1,000 miles from the capital of Juneau, she spent a decade in the state legislature. She was elected to Congress in a special election in 2022 to replace Mr. Young after his death and was elected later that year to a full term. She was the first Democrat to hold the seat in a half-century, the first woman to represent Alaska in the U.S. House and the first Alaska Native ever elected to Congress. She lost her seat in 2024.

Ms. Peltola, has been married three times. Her third husband, Eugene “Buzzy” Peltola Jr., was killed in 2023 when a small Piper PA 18-150 Super Cub he was piloting crashed in the mountains of southwestern Alaska. The cause, according to the accident report: an overload of moose meat and antlers attached to the side of the plane.

When Ms. Peltola was in the Alaska Legislature, she started “Fish Fridays” — weekly get-togethers in her office at which she fed her colleagues salmon. She helped with grass-roots outreach during Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski’s write-in campaign in 2010. And when Ms. Peltola got to Congress, she hired several of Mr. Young’s staffers — Republicans — including his chief of staff. She is friends with Sarah Palin, the former Alaska governor and Republican vice-presidential nominee, who once called Ms. Peltola a “real Alaskan chick.” During her time on Capitol Hill, Ms. Peltola was the co-chair of the Blue Dog Coalition for Policy, the caucus of centrist Democrats. “I certainly wouldn’t call myself a liberal,” she once said.

Ms. Peltola is one of the top recruits of Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, who has called her “the final piece of the puzzle” in the Democrats’ efforts to regain control the chamber — but Ms. Peltola is running against Washington as much as she is any of her opponents.

In her campaign pitch, she targeted “the rigged system in D.C. that’s shutting down Alaska while politicians feather their own nest.”

“No one from the Lower 48 is coming to save us,” she said.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Dan Sullivan, the Alaska Senator Seeking Re-election
item.description:
Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, is seeking a third term in the Senate in a competitive race that also features a well-known Democratic challenger and a man who shares his name.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Sullivan, the junior senator from Alaska, who is competing on Tuesday in a nonpartisan primary in which the top four finishers advance to the November general election.

1. Mr. Sullivan lost a court battle to kick another Dan Sullivan off the ballot. He’s Senator Dan S. Sullivan. One of his opponents is Dan J. Sullivan, a retired fifth-grade teacher without much of a political background but with a lot of name recognition. The lesser-known Mr. Sullivan has said his aim is to unseat the incumbent senator, but he has done little campaigning. Republicans fear that voters could confuse the two, and have accused Democrats of planting the second Sullivan to divide votes in what could be a close race. Democrats in the state, including the leading candidate in the race, have denied the accusations. Mr. Sullivan, the senator, brought the battle to court, but he ultimately lost in June, when the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Dan J. Sullivan could appear on the ballot, giving voters two Sullivans to choose from.

2. The senator faces a strong Democratic challenger. Alaska has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly two decades, but the conservative-leaning state has long inched toward the political center, and most Alaska voters are politically unaffiliated. A state poll has shown that former Representative Mary Peltola — a well-funded Democrat making an appeal to working-class, independent and Native voters — is competitive. National Democrats view Alaska as a must-win if they are to retake the Senate. The Cook Political Report considers the race a tossup.

3. President Trump has endorsed Mr. Sullivan. The senator has been a reliable supporter of Mr. Trump, including on the Iran war and sweeping tariffs, during the president’s second term. But Mr. Sullivan has occasionally broken ranks, voting with Democrats against Mr. Trump’s plans for a new White House ballroom and an effort to set up an “anti-weaponization” fund. Still, he is far more tethered to the right than Senator Lisa Murkowski, the state’s senior senator, a Republican moderate and a longtime party swing voter who has criticized Mr. Trump. “Sullivan may have positioned himself a little too far to the right for a lot of Alaskans,” said Glenn Wright, a political scientist at the University of Alaska Southeast. Mr. Sullivan’s ties to Trump could cause re-election troubles in Alaska, Mr. Wright said, given inflation and rising oil prices under the president, particularly in a state with a high cost of living.

4. He once worked in the State Department under President George W. Bush. Mr. Sullivan, 61, is a Marine veteran with a long track record in government. He was the assistant secretary of state for economic, energy and business affairs under President Bush from 2006 to 2009. Mr. Sullivan also served as Alaska’s attorney general and as commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources before first winning his Senate seat in 2014. “Alaska has a history of politicians with big personalities,” Mr. Wright said. “Sullivan, by all accounts, is quietly competent.”

5. He has emphasized his local endorsements. Mr. Sullivan features a picture with Mr. Trump on his campaign website, but he does not include the president in his list of endorsements. The incumbent has earned the support of the largest commercial fishing organization in the state, labor unions and a group representing Alaska Native corporations. He has been a staunch proponent of major oil and mining projects.

item.title: A Stunning Win for the Left in Florida: 6 Takeaways From Tuesday’s Primaries
item.description:
State Representative Angie Nixon, a progressive firebrand who ran such an underdog campaign that she could not afford a single television ad, won the Democratic Senate nomination in Florida on Tuesday in a shocking upset.

With her defeat of Alex Vindman, a candidate with establishment backing who raised more than 16 times as much campaign money, Ms. Nixon, a democratic socialist, continued the left’s winning streak this year in Democratic primaries.

Florida had appeared impervious to the prevailing political winds in recent election cycles, with Republicans doing exceptionally well in the state in 2022, in what was otherwise a strong year for Democrats. Ms. Nixon’s breakthrough victory, and losses by Republicans endorsed by President Trump in several Florida congressional primaries, suggested that maybe Florida is no longer quite as immune to national trends.

Here are six takeaways from Tuesday night’s primaries in Florida, Alaska and Wyoming, and a special election in California:

Money is usually key to political campaigns in Florida, the nation’s third-largest state and home to 10 television markets. Ms. Nixon raised only $975,000, compared to Mr. Vindman’s more than $16.3 million. And she spent just $60,000 on advertising, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm, compared to his $2.2 million.

Mr. Vindman will face questions about why his campaign did not spend more introducing him to voters. But credit Ms. Nixon, a union organizer, for knowing how to harness the enthusiasm of grass-roots Democrats and volunteers — and deftly using social media — to inform them about her candidacy.

A final weekend push in South Florida, home to many Democratic voters even as much of the region has trended toward Republicans, appears to have paid off: Ms. Nixon, who is from Jacksonville, defeated Mr. Vindman in Miami-Dade County, the state’s most populous, and in neighboring Broward County, where he lives.

Some of the most exciting elections for Florida Democrats over the past 20 years featured Black progressives named Barack Obama, who won the state twice, and Andrew Gillum, the former mayor of Tallahassee who lost a governor’s race by a hair in 2018. Ms. Nixon will surely try to learn from the coalitions they built and capitalize on the excitement that propelled her big win.

But neither Mr. Obama nor Mr. Gillum entered the general election with so little name recognition, campaign organization or money, all of which are needed to reach Florida’s giant and varied electorate.

Also: How will the democratic socialist label play? Ms. Nixon joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June, though the D.S.A. has not endorsed her candidacy. And Florida has gotten redder since Mr. Obama won the state in the 2008 and 2012 presidential races and Mr. Gillum narrowly lost the 2018 governor’s race. Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent who faced no serious primary opposition on Tuesday, is sitting on more than $8 million in campaign funds.

Representative Byron Donalds, who has long had Mr. Trump’s endorsement in the president’s adopted home state, crushed his rivals in the Republican primary for Florida governor. He has far out-raised the Democratic nominee, former Representative David Jolly, a former Republican.

But Mr. Donalds did not break 50 percent on Tuesday, as some Florida Republicans had hoped. And he did not win some largely white, rural counties in North Florida. Mr. Donalds is Black. Some Republicans will be looking at his underperformance in those counties with concerns about whether some white Republicans will be unwilling to vote for a Black nominee, choosing to stay home in November instead.

Mr. Donalds dismissed concerns that he had not won a majority of the vote, telling reporters he would earn that support.

“They want the same thing we all want,” he said of Republicans who voted for his rivals. “We want a Florida that is based on common sense, law and order, freedom.”

Representative Cory Mills lost the Republican primary in Florida’s Seventh Congressional District to Ryan Elijah, a former local television news anchor, after Mr. Mills lost key support within his own party. Two House colleagues endorsed Mr. Elijah, saying they could not risk losing the Republican-leaning seat with a weak candidate.

Mr. Mills faced a House Ethics Committee investigation related to allegations of assault and threatening behavior toward women. His ouster followed that of Representative Chuck Edwards of North Carolina, who was accused of sexually harassing two female former staffers and announced on Aug. 5 that he would not seek re-election. The next day, Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee lost a primary after drawing criticism for anti-Muslim remarks.

Representatives Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Jared Moskowitz, both moderate, pro-Israel Democrats, easily fended off rivals after Republican gerrymandering led them to compete in new districts. Ms. Wasserman Schultz, an 11-term incumbent, overcame frustration from Black Democrats who did not want her to represent a historically Black district. Mr. Moskowitz bested a democratic socialist.

Most of the state is four hours behind the East Coast. Patience is a virtue.

Shane Goldmacher, David Ovalle and Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

item.title: Peltola and Sullivan Advance in Crucial Alaska Senate Contest
item.description:
A high-profile Senate race in Alaska is officially set: Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former congresswoman, and Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, advanced from the state’s top-four nonpartisan primary on Tuesday night local time, according to The Associated Press. They will face off in November in a race that could determine control of the Senate.

Ms. Peltola was seen as the only Democrat who could pose a formidable challenge to Mr. Sullivan, a two-term incumbent running in a conservative state known for its independent streak. An Alaska Native, Ms. Peltola is a former commercial fisher and a former state legislator. She rose to political stardom with an upset win for the state’s only House seat in 2022, becoming the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the House in decades.

Both candidates have significant resources at their disposal as their parties gear up for a highly competitive sprint to November. Mr. Sullivan, a Marine veteran who is a supporter of President Trump, has forged strong bonds with the state’s various constituencies during his tenure in the Senate, including Native and fishing groups. But he faces headwinds given Alaska’s high cost of living and citizens’ frustrations with the current administration.

One wild card still to be determined is whether a different primary candidate also named Dan Sullivan will advance to the four-person general election ballot. This Mr. Sullivan, a retired teacher from the tiny fishing village of Petersburg, drew criticism from Republicans who decried his candidacy as a Democratic trick meant to confuse voters and split votes with the sitting senator. The Republican-run state elections division removed him from the ballot this summer before being overruled by the courts.

The lesser-known Mr. Sullivan has insisted that his long-shot bid is legitimate and not a ruse. If he advances to the ballot in November, he could play a spoiler role in a state with just about 600,000 registered voters.

Ms. Peltola claimed early momentum this spring after entering the race, but her campaign hit some snags in recent days. Last week, she distanced herself from former Vice President Kamala Harris, who sent out a fund-raising appeal on Ms. Peltola’s behalf that threatened to undermine Ms. Peltola’s image as an independent-minded candidate unaffiliated with national Democrats or politics in the Lower 48.

Her campaign also underwent a staffing shake-up last week, as she fired several longtime campaign aides and contractors and swapped out campaign managers.

item.title: Progressive Democrat Makes Runoff for Alaska Governor
item.description:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who entered politics as a teenager on Howard Dean’s presidential campaign, won the chance to become the youngest governor in Alaska history by securing one of four spots in the November general election, The Associated Press said.

Another Democrat, Tom Begich, also secured one of the four spots, according to The A.P.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old Democrat, pitched himself as the only candidate capable of bringing together Democrats, Republicans and unaffiliated voters to solve Alaska’s fiscal crisis and population loss. As a five-term Democratic state legislator from Sitka, Alaska, he represented a southeastern district that Republican presidential candidates have consistently won.

He was among the top fund-raisers in the 17-candidate primary, raising much of his money from out-of-state donors linked to the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, but he also campaigned hard in rural Alaska. That included driving a snowmobile to the Arctic Ocean and riding a skiff 450 miles down the Yukon River.

“We’re potentially at a moment where the next governor and the next Legislature will be making decisions similar to the start of the pipeline here,” he said in an interview last month, referring to the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, built five decades ago. “It’s going to take a different approach to do this right.”

He and the three other top finishers will compete in a November election that will use ranked-choice voting. Alaskans are selecting a successor to Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican barred from seeking a third term.

Alaskans have backed President Trump in the last three presidential races, but unaffiliated voters outnumber both Republicans and Democrats, and the Legislature has been governed for nearly a decade by a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents.
