item.title: He Bet Big on Trump. The Prize Could Be the Florida Governor’s Mansion.
item.description:
In 2010, a young father, still smarting about the 2008 financial crisis, was at a Tea Party protest in Naples, Fla., railing against what he called the excesses of liberal politics.

“I stand before a sea of conservative patriots who seek to take the reins of power from the progressive left,” he declared.

Byron Donalds stood out that day, a Black conservative in an overwhelmingly white and wealthy community, and he knew how to seize the political moment. His involvement in the insurgent right-wing movement eventually propelled him to elective office in 2016.

By 2023, Mr. Donalds was a Republican member of Congress, and this time, he took a gamble, endorsing Donald J. Trump over Florida’s Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, in the party’s presidential primary when the DeSantis star appeared to be on the rise.

The payoff was huge. A month after President Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he backed Mr. Donalds to be the next governor of Florida, the president’s adopted home state, before he had even declared his candidacy. On Tuesday, Mr. Donalds, 47, easily captured the Republican nomination to lead the nation’s third largest state, making him the front-runner in the November general election against David Jolly, the Democratic nominee. Democrats have not held the Florida governor’s mansion in more than a quarter century, but Republicans face national headwinds in the midterms, which Mr. Jolly has tried to capitalize on as he has crisscrossed the state.

If elected, Mr. Donalds would become Florida’s first Black governor and the first Republican Black governor since Reconstruction, though he prefers not to talk about his race. Florida, he said in an interview at his campaign headquarters in Naples last week, is a “great meritocracy.” Voters, he added, “just want the best person that’s going to do the job.”

His biggest challenge may be governing in the wake of Mr. DeSantis, a popular but divisive two-term governor who turned Florida into a laboratory for the political right — all while residents struggled with soaring housing costs and stubborn inflation.

While Mr. Donalds has campaigned on “defending the Florida dream” by lowering home insurance rates, among other things, he has shown little interest in departing from Mr. DeSantis’s policies broadly. The question for Floridians was “not so much what’s different,” he said, “but it’s really about what comes next.”

Mr. Donalds described the importance of modernizing state agencies with technology to improve efficiency. He rarely veered into the culture war issues that have defined Mr. DeSantis.

Yet his political action committee has already aired campaign commercials attacking Mr. Jolly as “radically liberal” for supporting transition care for transgender children.

Mr. Donalds has also backed legislation to push public education funds to charter or private schools and give parents and outside groups a bigger say in school curriculums. His wife, Erika, created a company and a nonprofit that took advantage of the expansion of charter schools and voucher programs in Florida and grew the couple’s wealth, according to their financial disclosures.

Stylistically, he is more approachable and upbeat than the prickly, combative Mr. DeSantis, who for years got Republican state lawmakers to bend to his will by using endorsements, vetoes and executive power as cudgels. Mrs. Donalds said that will be welcomed in Tallahassee.

“I think a lot of the lawmakers, especially those that he’s served with in the past, are looking forward to his administration because of the way he works with people,” she said of her husband in an interview last week. “He wants everyone to win.”

One of three siblings, Mr. Donalds grew up in Crown Heights, Brooklyn. His single mother, Meredith Brown, toiled to put food on the table but paid for him to attend Catholic school.

Ms. Brown said in an interview that her focus on education helped turn her son into a voracious childhood reader. She affectionately called her son “my nerd.”

He took a Greyhound bus to Florida and attended Florida A&M University, a historically Black school, before transferring to Florida State University, both in Tallahassee. He married an on-and-off girlfriend and classmate; she later told the Florida Trident that they married only so she could get cheaper, in-state tuition.

During his young adulthood, he sold what he has described as small amounts of marijuana to make ends meet. He was charged with marijuana possession, a case that was dropped after he completed a program for first-time offenders. He was arrested in connection with what he later said was a bank-card fraud scheme, a case that was also dropped and later sealed from his record.

At Florida State, he joined a business fraternity and met Erika Lees, a sixth-generation Floridian from the Tampa area, who is now his wife. She encouraged him to go to church.

He was 21 when, while waiting tables at Cracker Barrel one day, he served a group of customers returning from a religious revival. Mr. Donalds has said that as he rolled silverware, he felt a call from God to stop running from his faith. He hurried outside, met the departing religious group he had just served, and prayed with them.

Mr. Donalds and his new wife settled in Naples, where they both worked in the finance sector, had three sons and became youth leaders at a nondenominational Christian church. Mr. Donalds coached youth basketball and football.

“He’s kind of portrayed himself as a Black Horatio Alger, someone who has pulled himself up by his bootstraps,” said Peter J. Bergerson, a professor emeritus of political science at Florida Gulf Coast University who has followed Mr. Donalds’ political career.

Mr. Donalds’s interest in politics began with the financial crisis. While working on an investment report for work, he said in the interview, he grew angry watching a House Financial Services Committee hearing.

“They just didn’t know what they were talking about,” he recalled. “It was frustrating.”

Mr. Donalds soon began reading books on economic theory, he and his wife said. He watched less ESPN and more CNBC. By 2010, Mr. Donalds had joined the Naples Tea Party.

The movement, which objected to big government spending and financial bailouts under the Obama administration, faced accusations of racism, Mr. Donalds recalled. At one Tea Party rally, two older white women asked to take a photograph with him. He asked why.

“‘Because we want to prove to our friends that we’re not racists,’” Mr. Donalds recalled them saying.

As Tea Party candidates racked up electoral victories, Mr. Donalds mounted his first campaign for Congress in 2012 — and lost. But he made an impression, said Neil G. Volz, a political activist who met Mr. Donalds at a candidate forum that year.

“You just could see the political skills that he had right out the gate,” he said.

In 2016, Mr. Donalds won a seat in the Florida Legislature. He would go on to support a ballot measure in 2018 that would restore many felons’ voting rights, a campaign that Mr. Volz helped lead.

That year, Mr. Donalds went on cable news to defend Mr. DeSantis, then the Republican nominee for governor, after he was accused of using a racist dog whistle against his Democratic opponent, Andrew Gillum, who was Black.

His relationship with Mr. DeSantis fractured five years later.

As the 2024 presidential election approached, Florida Republicans were divided over whether to support Mr. Trump, whose re-election seemed uncertain, or Mr. DeSantis, who became a conservative darling during the coronavirus pandemic.

Mr. Donalds’s prominence had risen after he was elected to Congress in 2020 and became a go-to guest on conservative news shows. In 2023, he objected to the DeSantis administration’s proposed rewrite of Black history standards for middle school, which said enslaved people “developed skills which, in some instances, could be applied for their personal benefit.”

Mr. Donalds endorsed Mr. Trump. Mr. DeSantis responded by saying that Mr. Donalds had not played much of a role in the state’s conservative policy triumphs.

Mr. Donalds has continued to publicly praise Mr. DeSantis as the “best governor in the country.” But the president’s endorsement of Mr. Donalds for governor effectively denied Mr. DeSantis the power to name a political heir.

Last year, the governor weighed whether his wife, Casey, should run to succeed him. He also appointed an ally, Jay Collins, as lieutenant governor, but then declined to back him — or anyone else — for governor.

But Mr. Donalds, who raised more than $100 million over the course of the campaign, looked unbeatable.

Mike Durante, 76, a pastor who attended a Donalds rally at a veterans’ hall in Naples last week, said the choice was simple.

“I support Trump,” he said. “And he supports Trump.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: U.S. Will Try California Arson Suspect Again After Stunning Mistrial
item.description:
Federal prosecutors are trying again to convict a 30-year-old man accused of starting one of the most destructive fires in California history, recasting the charges against him after a stunning mistrial.

The effort reflects a push for accountability after the deadly 2025 Palisades fire, even after 10 of 12 jurors voted in June to find the man, Jonathan Rinderknecht, not guilty. A federal judge declared a mistrial.

Prosecutors filed a new indictment on Aug. 13, shaving the number of arson-related felony charges against Mr. Rinderknecht from three to two. One now focuses solely on the Lachman fire, which began on New Year’s and which investigators say smoldered for a week before exploding into the Palisades blaze.

Mr. Rinderknecht now faces felony charges of one count of destruction of property using fire — specifically the Lachman fire — and one of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce, which relates to both the Lachman and Palisades fires.

An arraignment is scheduled Wednesday in a downtown Los Angeles federal courtroom before Judge Anne Hwang of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. Mr. Rinderknecht’s retrial is set to begin Oct. 19.

At Mr. Rinderknecht’s first trial, the prosecution argued that Mr. Rinderknecht had resented the rich and started the fire with a lighter as “societal revenge.”

But Mr. Rinderknecht’s lawyer argued that New Year’s fireworks had set it off.

Prosecutors said that Mr. Rinderknecht had been angry that he hadn’t secured plans for the holiday, and his Uber passengers from that night testified that he ranted about capitalism. Late that night, Mr. Rinderknecht hiked up a Pacific Palisades trail near where the Lachman fire began.

As the blaze grew, he called 911 more than a dozen times. Prosecutors said he was trying to cover his tracks. Mr. Rinderknecht’s lawyer, Steven Haney, said it would be “self-destructive and idiotic” for an arsonist to call the authorities rather than leaving immediately.

Mr. Haney at the trial said there were gaps in the government’s case. The scene was left unprotected for 12 days, destroying evidence; of 9,000 or so videos compiled in the investigation, none caught the ignition; and no one identified the exact time the fire started, he said.

To Dave Ring, a Los Angeles-based civil lawyer who has no interest in the case, the revised charges represent a “distinction without a difference” and prosecutors will still face steep challenges.

“I think their case still is going to be incredibly difficult to win,” he said.

Regardless of the outcome of Mr. Rinderknecht’s case, the city of Los Angeles and other government agencies could still face civil liability for failures during the fire.

Many residents are still displaced more than a year and a half after the fire killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes in the wealthy Pacific Palisades section of Los Angeles.

item.title: The Left Notches Another Win With This Secret Weapon: Old-Fashioned Organizing
item.description:
Four days before Tuesday’s Democratic Senate primary, State Representative Angie Nixon did what she has always done in Florida: Organize activists.

The group of volunteers for her underdog Senate campaign sat inside a union office in suburban Broward County, a liberal stronghold in the increasingly Republican-leaning state. It was a small group, maybe a dozen people.

But don’t worry, Ms. Nixon’s political director, Rachel Gilmer, reassured them: “This tiny room is part of many, many tiny rooms” across the state, she said, with more volunteers also ready to knock on Democratic voters’ doors.

Ms. Nixon, 42, walked in, wearing a big smile and dressed in her signature hot pink, the same color splashed on her van, campaign signs and fliers. She rallied her limited troops.

“This is a people-powered movement,” she told the volunteers, “that is built on the shoulders of working families, on the shoulders of union workers, on the shoulders of folks who have been marginalized for so long.”

Ms. Nixon proved she was right on Tuesday, defeating Alex Vindman, the presumed front-runner, in a stunning upset that energized progressive Democrats in Florida for the first time in years. She won as other candidates from the political left have done across the country, by focusing on the grass roots. She did it with incredibly limited resources.

The flip side to Ms. Nixon’s victory is that it may turn what was widely seen as a long-shot goal for Democrats — defeating a sitting Republican senator in comfortably red Florida — into an even longer shot. The Cook Political Report has consistently rated the race this year as “solid R.”

For now, the left is rejoicing in Ms. Nixon’s triumph. And others are examining the outcome to figure out how the heck she did it.

The huge disparity between her fund-raising and Mr. Vindman’s was nowhere to be seen in the results. Ms. Nixon won by 12 percentage points, besting Mr. Vindman in every major metropolitan area except West Palm Beach. She won big not only in Duval County, where she lives, in Jacksonville, but also in Miami-Dade County, the state’s most populous, and in Broward County, where Mr. Vindman lives.

“If you’re from Broward, you can’t lose Broward and Dade,” Mitchell Berger, a Fort Lauderdale lawyer who has been a major Democratic fund-raiser for decades, said on Tuesday night at Mr. Vindman’s election night event, as his loss left attendees looking bewildered. “You can’t lose your home area.”

Ms. Nixon also did particularly well in areas with high concentrations of young voters and progressives, including Gainesville, where the University of Florida is, and Tallahassee, home of Florida State University.

A three-term state lawmaker and mother of five, she joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June, though the group has not endorsed her candidacy. Even before then, she was known as a progressive firebrand and thorn in the side of Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican. This year, she staged a sit-in at the governor’s office in the State Capitol to protest a Republican gerrymander of the state’s congressional map. She was eventually arrested and removed from the office. She also interrupted a State House vote on the map by protesting with a bullhorn.

The incident drew a reprimand from state lawmakers — but also some attention to her Senate candidacy. She chronicled much of her campaign online, as she drove herself from one event to another in a van. At one point, she shared video as she figured out how to change a flat tire.

Over the summer, Mr. Vindman’s campaign stumbled twice. During a Democratic Party fund-raiser gala, he fled from a group of social media influencers, in what later appeared to have been a miscommunication. But the video was not flattering for a first-time candidate still little-known to many Democratic voters.

Then, his wife, Rachel Vindman, wrote a social media post using a vulgar term that, without naming Ms. Nixon, appeared to insult her and mock her clothes and shoes. Ms. Vindman deleted the post and apologized, but not before it angered many grass-roots Democrats. (Ms. Nixon, who campaigned in sneakers, later posted a photo of heeled sandals with the caption: “Are these ok?”)

Last week, as the final weekend of early voting approached, Ms. Nixon and two House candidates running as democratic socialists planned a big weekend in South Florida. Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan joined them on the trail and at a rally for Gen Z voters. The rally changed venues because of pressure over Ms. Tlaib’s and Ms. Nixon’s anti-Israel stance in Broward County, which has a large Jewish population.

At the union hall in Miramar, where her volunteers gathered on Friday afternoon, Ms. Nixon said the fallout over the rally suggested Democrats were running “scared.”

In a brief interview that day, she did not predict victory. Her campaign did not have money to poll, she acknowledged, and no public polls had been conducted in the primary race. She could not know exactly where she stood against Mr. Vindman.

But she knew Mr. Vindman’s campaign had polled at least once. He had not spent money attacking her, which many Florida Democrats assumed meant he was not worried about her candidacy. Ms. Nixon, however, noted that his campaign had also not released its internal poll, suggesting that perhaps the race was closer than expected.

By the time the rally began, late into the night at a downtown Fort Lauderdale wine bar packed with hundreds of mostly young people, including social media influencers, Ms. Nixon was losing her voice.

“Throughout this country’s 250 years, every time we have been faced with oppression, we have matched it with resistance,” she told the crowd, urging them to spend the last few days of the campaign mobilizing. “We have nothing to lose.”

Susan Cooper Eastman contributed reporting from Jacksonville, Fla.; David Ovalle from Orlando, Fla., and Ruth Igielnik from New York.
